name: Shisochin
description: Shisochin significa “quattro aberturas” ou “quatro direções”. O kata caracteriza-se por muitas e potentes técnicas de mão aberta e enfatiza o combate em quatro direções.

origin.title: Origin
origin.content: Shisochin likely originated in Okinawa before Higaonna's China trip. There is a historical record from 1867 of Seisho Aragaki demonstrating a kata called "Chisaukin", presumably the predecessor of Shisochin. Aragaki was Higaonna's teacher, so Shisochin has Okinawan roots. Possibly Higaonna or even Miyagi himself later brought in a refined form of Shisochin. Additionally, research (Akio Kinjo) points to strong similarities with Southern Chinese mantis/cricket style. The kata appears to be a synthesis of Aragaki's techniques (comparable to his kata Unsū) and Asian mantis postures.

transmission.title: Transmission to Goju-Ryu
transmission.content: Chōjun Miyagi undoubtedly learned Shisochin (possibly through Aragaki or Higaonna) and passed it on within Goju-Ryu. Kenjiro Iguchi (Gojukai) says it was one of the classical kata that came to Naha-te through Higaonna, and Miyagi included it in the Goju curriculum. Shito-Ryu also has a similar form (learned by Mabuni from Aragaki's legacy). Tōon-Ryū does not use Shisochin, which supports the hypothesis that Miyagi arranged it from Okinawa.

historicalDevelopment.title: Historical development and variations
historicalDevelopment.content: Shisochin is one of the most "symmetrical" Goju kata, with a high proportion of soft, open-hand techniques. The kata has undergone few fundamental changes since its beginning; variations are limited to style differences (e.g., in Shito-ryu or Kyokushin). The numbering (as 'The fourth kata') remains consistent. The hypothesis is that Miyagi established Shisochin based on Okinawan heritage (looking at Aragaki's Unsū and Rohai) and possibly streamlined it with influences from southern mantis. Historically, Shisochin thus differs from typical hard kata through its open-handed nukite movements.

technicalFeatures.title: Technical and philosophical characteristics
technicalFeatures.content: Shisochin begins with three consecutive nukite (finger strikes) from sanchin-dachi. Then it is worked "symmetrically", without favoring any side, and contains many soft, circular movements. Important techniques: rising elbow strikes, tie Uke (pulling blocks with the palm), haito-uke (stopping hand blocks), and turning movements in all directions. Philosophically, it is seen as a kata of balance ("fighting in all directions at once"), which could reflect the name. The breathing is generally more normal than in Sanchin, but the movements have a flowing character.

controversy.title: Controversy/variations within Goju-Ryu
controversy.content: There is debate about the name and origin (mantis vs crane). Some translate it as "battle in four directions". Variants worldwide are minimal; the core movements remain the same across all Goju Ryu schools. Only in the Meibukan circuit is there talk of a third morote-tsuki at the end, but that applies more to Gekisai. Shisochin itself has few variants within Goju. However, Shisochin is performed as a free kata in some JKA competitions.

relationships.title: Relationship to other kata/systems
relationships.content: Shisochin belongs to the "southern kata" within Goju (alongside Saifa, Seiyunchin, Sepai, Kururunfa). It shows similarities with Aragaki's kata Unsū (same opening nukite) and with Tomari-Rohai (identical beginning). It shares characteristics with Chinese Fist styles (Southern White Crane and Mantis) through the combination of short attacks and circular movements. There is a certain link with Shito-Ryu's Rohai/Sochin and Isshin-Ryu's Rohai, indicating that Shisochin possibly reflects a common "Okinawan origin kata".

modernPractice.title: Use in modern practice
modernPractice.content: Shisochin is an advanced kata taught in advanced Goju lessons. It is practiced at demonstrations and internationally in kata competitions (same embusen as in traditional Goju). It plays a role in self-defense training (including elbow and gripping techniques). Since the kata appears less frequently in karate events, it remains primarily a traditional training form.

nameAndMeaning.title: Name and meaning
nameAndMeaning.content: The meaning of Shisochin (死相鎮 or 蟋蟀戦 according to theories) is disputed. A common translation is "crane fighting posture" or "crane fighting posture" (for example from the Chinese xishi grip). However, researchers suggest that the original characters were probably 蟋蟀戦 (chi-sau-kin, "cricket/mantis fight"). In Min Nan (Hokkien) this sounds like shisauchin, which in both dialects means "mantis fight". The name may thus refer to fighting principles from the Southern Chinese mantis style. Some explanations mention "battle on four fronts", but little evidence supports this. In summary, the symbolic character lies in the "four-direction battle" or the mantis-cricket theme.
